# Reconciling the simulation and the real data {#sec-reconcile}

The two halves of the study agree on the main point and disagree on two
details. Here we compare the real data with the simulation setting closest to
it (1% prevalence, $n = 20{,}000$, high separation); the full numbers are in
@tbl-real and Appendix @tbl-app-change.

The two halves agree on the main point. For the lasso, no remedy improves
ROC-AUC in either setting, and the threshold leaves the ranking alone in both,
by construction. Class weights hurt the forest in both, and in both every
remedy buys sensitivity by giving up precision.

They disagree in two places. On the real data the lasso remedies *lower*
PR-AUC by 0.05 to 0.19, about ten times more than in the simulation. And on
the real data over-sampling and SMOTE *improve* the forest's PR-AUC, whereas
in the simulation they made it worse. We see three reasons for this, two
about the data and one about our own design.

The first reason is that the real model is not logistic. In the simulation
the lasso is the true model, so rebalancing can only move the intercept and
the ranking cannot change [@prentice1979]. Real frauds are not generated by a
logistic model. When the model is wrong, reweighting the classes changes
which errors the fit tries hardest to avoid, so it changes the slopes as well
as the intercept, and on these data that makes the top of the ranking worse.
A second, smaller effect is also likely. Over-sampling and SMOTE are applied
before cross-validation, so copies or near-copies of the same fraud can end
up in both the training and the validation folds. Cross-validation then
underestimates the error of weak penalties and may choose too small a
$\lambda$. Under-sampling, the worst remedy for the lasso, keeps only 344 of
about 199,000 normal transactions, so its large loss is mostly the price of
throwing data away.

The second reason is that real frauds are probably clustered. In the
simulation, positives are spread smoothly along one direction
(@fig-simdata). Real frauds are more likely to come in small groups of
similar transactions, for example several charges on one stolen card, and
@fig-ccdata already showed that they bunch up at certain hours. A forest can
learn such pockets if it sees enough frauds, and SMOTE fills in the space
between nearby frauds, which suits this kind of structure. That would explain
why SMOTE helps the forest on the real data but not in the simulation. We
cannot check it directly, because the predictors are anonymous principal
components.

The third reason is our own forest set-up. To keep the run time manageable,
each real-data tree was grown on 20,000 rows rather than a full bootstrap
sample (@sec-realdata). The baseline training set has 344 frauds among about
199,000 rows, so a baseline tree sees only about
$20{,}000 \times 344 / 199{,}365 \approx 35$ frauds. After over-sampling or
SMOTE the training set is 50:50, so a tree sees about 10,000 positive rows.
Part of the forest's gain on the real data may therefore come from fixing a
"too few frauds per tree" problem that our own row limit created, and that
the simulated forests, which used full bootstrap samples, did not have. A
fairer test would give the baseline forest a stratified sample for each tree,
for example all the frauds plus 20,000 normal transactions. We did not have
time to run it and list it as further work.

The simulation therefore answers our question cleanly for the case it was
built for, a correct model with smoothly spread positives, and the real data
show what changes when those assumptions fail. Neither shows a case in which
resampling improves the lasso's ranking.
